Furthermore, if a monk is offered yellow myrobalan (gallnut) soaked in urine in one vessel and the 'four sweets' (catumadhura) in another, with the words, "Venerable sir, take whichever you wish," and even if his illness could be cured by either, he rejects the 'four sweets' and uses the gallnut as medicine, thinking, "Yellow myrobalan soaked in urine has been praised by the Buddhas and other virtuous ones." Such a monk is one of great contentment. This is his 'contentment with what is appropriate' (yathāsāruppasantuṭṭhi) regarding medicinal requisites.
152:
He is indeed very easily contented. This is his 'contentment with what is appropriate' (yathāsāruppasantosa) regarding medicinal requisites. Thus, referring to these three types of contentment, the Blessed One said: 'Monks, this Kassapa is contented with any kind of robe.'

'One who speaks in praise' (vaṇṇavādī) means: One monk might be contented himself but does not speak in praise of contentment. Another might not be contented himself but speaks in praise of contentment. Another is neither contented himself nor speaks in praise of contentment. Another is both contented himself and speaks in praise of contentment. To show that the Venerable Mahākassapa is like the fourth person, it was said: 'He is one who speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of robe.'

'Improper search' (anesana) refers to various types of improper livelihood, such as acting as a messenger, running errands, and so forth. 'Not obtaining' (aladdhā) means because of not receiving. Some monks, thinking 'How shall I obtain a robe?', associate with meritorious monks and, practicing hypocrisy (kuhana), become agitated and anxious. This Venerable Mahākassapa, even when not obtaining a robe, does not reach a state of alarm through exhaustion. 'Having obtained' (laddhā ca) means receiving in accordance with the Dhamma and fairness. 'Unattached' (agadhita) means being free from the greed of attachment. 'Not infatuated' (amucchita) means not falling into infatuation through excessive craving. 'Not overwhelmed' (anajjhāpanna) means not being covered, enveloped, or entangled by craving. 'Seeing the danger' (ādīnavadassāvī) means seeing the danger both in the offense of improper search and in attached consumption. 'Wise in the way of escape' (nissaraṇapañño) means consuming while knowing only the purpose of escape from the round of suffering, as stated: 'Only for the sake of warding off cold.' This is the meaning.

In phrases such as 'with any kind of almsfood,' the meaning should be understood as contentment with whatever almsfood, whatever lodging, or whatever medicinal requisites for the sick are obtained. In the statement, 'Monks, I will exhort you by Kassapa,' it means 'exhorting by Kassapa' because He says: 'Just as the Elder Mahākassapa is contented with the three types of contentment regarding the four requisites, you too should be like that.' In the statement, 'or by one who is like Kassapa,' it means 'exhorting by one like Kassapa' because He says: 'If there is another who, like the Elder Mahākassapa, is contented with the three types of contentment regarding the four requisites, you too should be like him.'

'One should practice to be like that' means: 'To teach the practice of effacement (sallekha) mentioned in this Santuṭṭhi Sutta is the responsibility of the Buddha; to fulfill this practice is our responsibility; one should carry out the responsibility that has arrived.' Thinking thus, the meaning is: 'You should practice to be like that, just as I have taught.' This concludes the commentary on the first sutta.

In the second sutta, 'one who possesses ardor' (ātāpī) refers to that right effort (sammāvāyāma) which burns away the defilements; with that...
153:
'To fulfill this practice of effacement is also our burden. Indeed, one should take up the burden that has come before one.' Thinking thus, [the Buddha said]: 'You, dear sons, should also practice for such a state to arise, just as I have taught.' The commentary on the first sutta is finished.

## 2. Anottappī Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, 'lacking ardor' (anātāpī) refers to one who is devoid of that right effort (sammāvāyāma) which burns away the defilements. 'Lacking dread' (anottappī) refers to one who is without fear regarding the arising of defilements and the non-arising of wholesome states. 'For enlightenment' (sambodhāya) means for the sake of knowing and blossoming through the Noble Path. 'For Nibbāna' (nibbānāya) means for the sake of realizing Nibbāna. 'For the unsurpassed security from bondage' (anuttarassa yogakkhemassa) means for the sake of the fruit of Arahantship. That fruit of Arahantship is both unsurpassed and excellent, and it is secure from the four bondages (yogas).

In the terms beginning with 'unarisen' (anuppannā), they should be understood in the following way. To one who, having obtained a requisite such as a robe not previously obtained, or some pleasant object from a supporter, a fellow-resident, or a pupil, accepts that object unwisely (ayoniso) thinking 'It is beautiful, it is good'; or to one who unwisely adverts to some other previously unexperienced object in whatever way—evil unwholesome states such as greed arise. These states should be known as 'unarisen' (anuppannā) [unwholesome states]. This is because in the beginningless saṃsāra, there is no evil state that has never arisen before. Even regarding an object or base previously experienced, if it arises suddenly due to such an object/base—having not arisen before through natural wisdom, or through recitation and inquiry, or through any of the means of scriptural study, meditative work, or wise reflection—these unwholesome states should also be known as: 'Unarisen unwholesome states, if they should arise, would lead to harm.' Furthermore, those states which arise repeatedly regarding those very objects and bases and are not abandoned should be known as: 'Arisen unwholesome states, if they are not abandoned, would lead to harm.' This is the summary here. As for the detailed distinction between arisen and unarisen, and the entire method of abandoning and not abandoning, I have already stated it in the Visuddhimagga, in the Description of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision (Ñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddesa).

'Unarisen wholesome states in me' (anuppannā me kusalā dhammā) refers to the faultless states known as virtue, concentration, the path, and the fruit, which have not yet been obtained. 'Arisen' (uppannā) refers to the obtaining of those very states. 'If they should cease, they would lead to harm' (nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyuṃ) means it should be understood that if those states such as virtue should cease through decline and not arise again, they would lead to harm. In this sutta, mundane wholesome states decline; there is no decline for supramundane states. The Blessed One made this teaching by the power of this fourth Right Effort (Sammappadhāna): 'For the persistence of arisen wholesome states.' Otherwise, if the second path does not arise quickly, the first path that has ceased would lead to harm—this is how the meaning should be noted in this Pali. In this way, in this second sutta, the Blessed One taught the four Right Efforts by the power of insight (vipassanā) which is the preliminary stage of the Path.

3. In the third sutta, 'simile of the moon' (candūpamā) means like the moon. In what way is it similar? It is not similar in terms of roundness. Rather, when the moon travels through the sky, it does not form an intimacy with anyone...
154:
This teaching is given by the power of these Right Efforts (sammappadhāna). It should be understood here that if the second path does not arise quickly and the first path ceases, it would lead to disadvantage. Thus, in this sutta, these four Right Efforts are taught by the power of insight (vipassanā) which precedes the path. The second sutta is finished.

## 3. Candūpamasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, 'like the moon' (candūpamā) means being like the moon. In what way? Is it by being round? No. Rather, just as the moon, while traversing the sky, does not form intimacy, affection, attachment, liking, longing, or obsession with anyone, yet is not unloved or unpleasing to the multitude (i.e., it is beloved), you too should be like the moon, beloved and pleasing to many by not forming intimacy and so forth, and approach the four classes of families, such as the Khattiyas. Furthermore, just as the moon dispels darkness and spreads light, so too should you be like the moon by dispelling the darkness of defilements and spreading the light of knowledge. In such ways, the meaning should be understood here.

'Withdraws the body, withdraws the mind' means withdrawing or pulling away the body and mind by not forming such intimacy. A monk who does not live in the forest and also thinks sensual thoughts and so forth withdraws neither the body nor the mind. A monk who lives in the forest but thinks sensual thoughts withdraws only the body, not the mind. A monk who lives near a village but does not think sensual thoughts withdraws only the mind, not the body. But a monk who lives in the forest and does not think sensual thoughts withdraws both. Intending to show that one should approach families being of such a nature, he said, 'withdraws the body, withdraws the mind.'

'Always a newcomer' (niccanavaka) means always being like a new arrival or a guest. For example, a guest enters a house reached in order, and when the householders see him, they feel compassion, thinking, 'Our sons and brothers have gone abroad and traveled like this,' and they make him sit and feed him. As soon as he has eaten, [he says,] 'Your...
155:
...take the bowl,' and having requested thus, he gets up and departs. He does not form intimacy with those householders, nor does he manage their affairs. Likewise, you too, when entering a house reached in order, should receive the offerings given by people who are inspired by your deportment, and depart without intimacy with those lay followers and without being concerned with their affairs.

To clarify this state of being 'always a newcomer' (niccanavaka-bhāva), the story of the two brothers should be told. It is heard that two brothers from the village of Vasabha left and ordained. They were known as Elder Cūḷanāga and Elder Mahānāga. Having lived on Cittalapabbata for thirty years and attained Arahantship, they came [back] thinking, 'We will see our mother.' They stayed at the Vasabha Monastery and entered the mother's village for alms the next day. The mother also took out gruel with a ladle and poured it into the bowl of one elder. While looking at that elder, motherly affection for her son arose. Then she said to him, 'Dear, are you my son Mahānāga?' The elder said, 'Laywoman, ask the elder coming behind,' and departed. Having given gruel to the later elder, she asked, 'Dear, are you my son Cūḷanāga?' The elder said, 'Laywoman, why did you not ask the elder who went before?' and departed. Thus, a monk who has cut off intimacy even with his mother is called 'always a newcomer' (niccanavaka).

'Not impudent' (appagabbhā) means not being rude. It means being free from the eight types of physical impudence (kāyapāgabbhiya), the four types of verbal impudence (vacīpāgabbhiya), and the many types of mental impudence (manopāgabbhiya).

The eight types of physical impudence mean performing improper physical actions in the Sangha, a group, towards an individual, in the dining hall, the fire room, the bathing place, on the alms-round path, and when entering a house. For example, some person in the midst of the Sangha sits clasping the knees or with a cloth wrapped around the knees, or sits with legs crossed, and so forth. Likewise in the midst of a group. 'In the midst of a group' means in an assembly of the fourfold community or in an assembly of a group studying the Suttantas and so forth. Likewise towards senior persons.

In the dining hall, it is not giving seats to elders or preventing juniors from taking seats. Likewise in the fire room, it is lighting a fire and so forth without asking the elders. In the bathing place, although it is said, 'One should bathe in the order of arrival without making a distinction between junior and senior,' one who disregards this, comes later, enters the water forcibly, and disturbs or harrasses the seniors and juniors.

On the alms-round path, [it is taking] the best seat...
156:
He goes ahead, jostling with his arms, to obtain the first water and the first alms-food. When entering a house, he enters ahead of the elders. He engages in physical play with the juniors. Such actions are known as (bodily impudence).

Verbal impudence (vacīpagabbhiya), which has four aspects, refers to uttering improper words in the midst of the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual, as well as inside a house. In this regard, a certain person in this Sasana preaches the Dhamma in the midst of the Saṅgha without asking permission. Likewise, in the midst of a group as previously mentioned, or in the presence of an individual, when questioned by people in that same place, he answers without asking permission from the elders. Inside a house, however, he says things such as, "What does such-and-such a person have? Is there gruel, or is there hard food or soft food? What will you give me? What shall we chew today? What shall we eat? What shall we drink?"

Mental impudence (manopagabbhiya), which has many aspects, refers to the thinking of sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka) and so forth in various places, even without committing transgressions through body or speech. Furthermore, the evil desire of one who is immoral, thinking, "Let people know me as one who is virtuous," is also called mental impudence. Thus, He says, "Approach [families] being unimpertinent (appagabbha) due to the absence of all these forms of impudence."

'Jarudapāna' means an old well. 'Pabbatavisama' means an uneven precipice on a mountain. 'Nadīvidugga' means a place with a broken bank at a river. "Without drawing back the body" means that a person who is fond of playing and so forth in such places looks on with affection, without drawing back his body, without making it heavy on one side, without maintaining his balance against the wind, and without drawing back his mind, because he does not see the danger, thinking, "If I fall here, I will suffer broken limbs and so forth," and thus he is not frightened. That person falls and meets with misfortune such as broken limbs. However, a person who desires to look because he wants water or for some other business, looks while drawing back his body, making it heavy on one side, maintaining his balance against the wind, and also drawing back his mind, being frightened by seeing the danger. That person does not fall; having looked as much as he desires, he departs happily wherever he wishes.
157:
In the phrase 'Even so' (evameva kho), there is this comparison between the simile and the subject. The four types of families should be understood as the old well and so forth, and the monk should be understood as the man who looks. Just as the man who looks at the old well, the precipice, and so forth with an unrestrained body and mind falls there, even so, the monk who approaches families with unrestrained body and so forth becomes bound to those families; because of that bondage, he meets with various misfortunes such as the breaking of the feet of virtue (sīla). Just as the man with a restrained body and mind does not fall into that old well or precipice, even so, the monk who approaches families with a restrained body, restrained mind, restrained speech, and well-established mindfulness, having a restrained body and mind, does not become bound to those families.

When he is not so bound, just as the feet of the man who does not fall into the old well or precipice are not broken or destroyed, even so, the feet of virtue are not destroyed. Just as the hands are not broken or destroyed, even so, the hands of faith (saddhā) are not broken or destroyed. Just as the belly is not ruptured or cut, even so, the belly of concentration (samādhi) is not ruptured or cut. Just as the head is not cracked or broken, even so, the head of wisdom (ñāṇa) is not cracked or broken. Just as stumps and thorns do not pierce that man, even so, the thorns of lust (rāga) and so forth do not pierce this monk. Just as that man, being free from danger, looks as much as he desires and departs happily wherever he wishes, even so, the monk, depending on families and making use of requisites such as robes, develops his meditation subject, contemplates conditioned formations (saṅkhāra), reaches Arahatship, and being happy with supramundane bliss, goes to the region of Nibbāna, where he has never been before, as he desires.

Now, a person of low inclination and wrong practice might say, "The Fully Enlightened One, having told us to abandon the three kinds of impudence and approach families being like the moon by being ever-new, places us in an impossible position, imposes an unbearable burden, and makes us do what cannot be done." To cut off the argument of such a person of wrong practice, and to show that "It is possible to do so; there is such a monk," He spoke the words beginning with, "Kassapa, O monks..."

"He moved his hand in the sky" means that he moved his hand in the lower part, the upper part, and on both sides, like one causing a double flash of lightning to move in the midst of the blue sky. This phrase is also known as an 'unbroken word' (asambhinnapada) in the Tipitaka, the Word of the Buddha. 'Attamano' means one with a delighted mind, one with his own mind, not one whose mind is seized by being cut off by dejection. This statement, "Kassapa, O monks," was also spoken in the same manner as before, to cut off the arguments of others and to show that "There is such a monk."
158:
"They should perform acts of devotion" means they should offer requisites such as robes and so forth. "They should practice for such a state" means they should practice for that unchanging state by fulfilling virtue where virtue is concerned, and by perfecting concentration, insight, the path, and the fruit where those respective states are concerned. "Anudaya" means the state of wanting to protect. "Anukampa" means the state of having a tender heart. Both of these are synonyms for compassion (karuṇā). "Monks, Kassapa..." This statement was also spoken, following the previous method, to cut off the arguments of others and to show that "there is such a monk." "Or with Kassapa..." In this context, the meaning should be understood as in the previous method, by connecting it with the simile of the moon and so forth. The third sutta is finished.

## 4. Kulūpaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, "Kulūpaka" means one who frequents the houses of families. "Let them give only to me" means let them give to me alone. "Sandīyati" means being weary or oppressed. The rest should be understood according to the method already stated. The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Jiṇṇa Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "Jiṇṇa" refers to the elder who is old. "Garukāni" (heavy) means that those robes, from the time they were received from the Teacher, became heavy due to being sewn with thread and patched in torn places, thus becoming many-layered. "Nibbasanāni" (discarded) is the name given because they were previously worn and then discarded by the Blessed One. "Therefore" means because you are old and have heavy rag-robes. "Robes given by householders" means he says, "Give up the practice of wearing rag-robes (paṃsukūlika-dhutaṅga) and wear robes given by householders." "Invited meals" means he says, "Give up the practice of eating only alms-food (piṇḍapātika-dhutaṅga) and enjoy invited meals such as food distributed by tickets (salāka-bhatta) and so forth." "And near me" means he says, "Give up the practice of forest-dwelling (āraññika-dhutaṅga) and live only in a monastery near a village."

Is it not the case that if a king appoints a general to the position of general, and while that general is pleasing the king with his duties such as serving the king, the king takes back that position and gives it to another, he is said to be doing something improper? In the same way, the Teacher traveled three gāvutas to meet the Elder Mahākassapa, sat at the foot of the Bahuputtaka banyan tree between Rājagaha and Nālandā, and ordained him with three exhortations. Then, did he not exchange his own robes with the elder and make him a forest-dweller and a rag-robe wearer from birth? If the Teacher, while being pleased by the elder's actions, out of a desire to act for the elder's sake, urged him to give up the rag-robe practice and so forth and to accept robes given by householders, would it not be said that the Teacher was doing something improper to the Elder Mahākassapa? This might be questioned. It would not be said that he did something improper. Why? Because he desired his welfare. Indeed, the Teacher had no desire for him to give up the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas). For example, just as musical instruments like a large drum do not make a sound if they are not struck, so too, the Teacher thought that such persons do not speak words like a lion's roar if they are not requested. With the intention of making him roar a lion's roar, he said, "Therefore, you, Kassapa..." and so forth. The elder also, in accordance with the Teacher's wish, roared a lion's roar by saying, "Venerable Sir, I am old, and I have lived in the forest for a long time," and so forth.
159:
Did not the Blessed One exchange his robes with the Elder Mahākassapa and cause him to undertake the forest-dweller's practice and the rag-robe wearer's practice from birth? If the Blessed One, while being pleased by the elder's actions, out of a desire to act for the elder's sake, urged him to give up the rag-robe practice and so forth and to accept robes given by householders, would it be said that he did something improper? It would not be said that he did something improper. Why? Because it was due to the power of desiring his welfare. In truth, the Blessed One did not wish for him to give up the ascetic practices. For example, just as musical instruments like a large drum do not make a sound if they are not struck, so too, the Blessed One thought that such persons do not roar a lion's roar if they are not requested. With the intention of making him roar a lion's roar, he spoke in this way. The Elder Mahākassapa also, in accordance with the Blessed One's wish, roared a lion's roar in this manner: "Venerable Sir, I am old, and I have lived in the forest for a long time," and so forth.

"Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra" means dwelling in happiness in the present life. This can only be obtained by one who dwells in the forest, not by one who dwells near a village. This is because one who dwells near a village hears the sounds of children, sees unsuitable sights, and hears unsuitable sounds. Because of seeing and hearing such things, dissatisfaction (anabhirati) arises in that monk. However, a monk dwelling in the forest, having entered the forest after traveling a gāvuta or half a yojana, hears the sounds of leopards, tigers, lions, and so forth. Because of hearing those sounds, a delight in seclusion (viveka) that is superior to human delight arises. With reference to this meaning, it was said:

"For the monk who has entered an empty place, who has a peaceful mind, and who clearly sees the Dhamma with insight, there is a delight that transcends that of humans."
"Whenever he contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates, he obtains joy and gladness; that is the Deathless for those who know it."
"Whether in front or behind, if no other person is found, there is comfort for one who delights alone in the forest."

Similarly, dwelling in happiness in the present life can only be obtained by a monk who collects alms-food, not by one who does not practice the alms-food eater's ascetic practice. A monk who does not practice the alms-food eater's practice tends to go at improper times, goes hurriedly, is restless, goes with anxiety, and has many doubts regarding that food. However, a monk who collects alms-food does not go at improper times, does not go hurriedly, is not restless, goes without anxiety, and does not have many doubts regarding that food.

How is this? A monk who does not practice the alms-food eater's practice, while dwelling in a monastery far from the village, thinks early in the morning, "Will I get gruel or leftover rice? At the dining hall or..."
160:
Specifically, a monk who does not practice the alms-food eater's ascetic practice (piṇḍapātika-dhutaṅga), thinking, 'I will receive something from the designated meals and so forth,' goes out very early in the morning, breaking spider webs and waking up sleeping herds of cattle (before they rise); when he goes thus, he is one who wanders at an improper time (akālacārī). To catch up with people who have left their homes for field work and such, he goes swiftly like a hunter chasing prey; when he goes thus, he is one who wanders hurriedly (turitacārī). If he sees someone on the way, he asks, 'Is such-and-such a male lay follower or such-and-such a female lay follower at home or not?' If he hears, 'They are not at home,' he thinks, 'Where will I get food now?' and trembles with anxiety like one being burned by fire. Even though he himself wishes to go to the west, if he receives a meal-ticket for the east, he approaches another monk who received a ticket for the west and says, 'Venerable sir, I will go to the west; please take my ticket and give yours to me,' thus exchanging the meal-ticket.

Alternatively, while taking and consuming one meal-ticket food, when people say, 'Give us the bowl for another person's meal-ticket food,' he says, 'Venerable sir, give me your bowl; I will put the food in my bowl and then give you your bowl,' thus having another monk's bowl brought, putting the food into his own bowl when it arrives, and returning the bowl; this is called 'exchanging the bowl.' In the monastery, kings, royal ministers, and others give great offerings. This monk has also received a meal-ticket for a more distant village. If he does not go there, he fears he will not receive a meal-ticket for the next seven days; out of fear of loss (alābhabhaya), he goes. A monk who goes in this way is said to go with worldly concern (palibuddha). When that monk goes for the sake of meal-ticket food and so forth, many doubts arise in him: 'Will they give to me or not? Or will they not give? Will they give fine food or coarse food? Will it be a little or a lot? Will it be cold or hot?'

However, a monk who observes the alms-food eater's ascetic practice (piṇḍapātika) rises early, performs his major and minor duties, attends to his body, enters his dwelling place, applies his mind to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), notes the time, and goes only when it is the proper time for the people to be able to offer alms with a ladle and so forth; therefore, he is not one who wanders at an improper time (akālacārī). Because he goes practicing insight (vipassanā) by dividing each footstep into six parts, he is not one who wanders hurriedly (turitacārī). Due to his own venerable nature, he does not ask, 'Is such-and-such a person at home or not?' He does not even accept meal-ticket food and the like. Since he does not accept them, what would he have to exchange? He is without worldly concern regarding the wishes of others...
161:
...and applying his mind to the meditation subject, he goes as he pleases. Unlike the other, he does not have many doubts. If he does not receive food in one village or one street, he wanders elsewhere. Even if he does not receive it there, while wandering elsewhere, when he obtains mixed alms-food, he consumes it as if it were nectar (amata) and goes on.

This benefit is obtained only by a rag-robe wearer (paṃsukūlika), not by one who is not a rag-robe wearer. For one who is not a rag-robe wearer wanders seeking rainy-season robes and does not seek a suitable lodging (senāsana). However, a rag-robe wearer does not need to wander seeking rainy-season robes and thus seeks only a suitable lodging. This is obtained only by a triple-robe wearer (tecīvarika), not by others. For one who is not a triple-robe wearer has many goods and requisites, and thus lacks a comfortable dwelling. It is obtained only by those with qualities such as fewness of wishes (appicchatā), not by others. Therefore, it is said: 'Seeing his own pleasant dwelling in this very life.' The fifth sutta ends.

## ၆။ ဩဝါဒသုတ်အဖွင့်

In the commentary on the sixth sutta, why did the Buddha say, 'Either I...'? It was for the purpose of establishing the Elder Mahākassapa in his own position. Was it because Sāriputta and Moggallāna were not there? They were there. However, the Buddha had this thought: 'These two, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, will not remain for long. But Kassapa will live to be one hundred and twenty years old. After I have attained Parinibbāna, he will sit in the Sattapaṇṇi Cave, conduct the Recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya (Dhamma-vinaya-saṅgaha), and make my Dispensation (Sāsana) endure for a period of five thousand years. I shall establish this Mahākassapa in my place; in this way, the monks will consider that Kassapa's words should be listened to.' Therefore, he spoke thus.

'Dubbacā' means those who are difficult to speak to with words of admonition. 'Dovacassakaraṇehi' means by those qualities that make one difficult to admonish. 'Appadakkhiṇaggāhino' refers to those who, even after hearing words of instruction, do not receive them respectfully and do not practice according to the instruction. He shows that those who do not practice are called 'those who grasp from the left' (vāmaggāhino). 'Accāvadante' means speaking overbearingly, referring to those who engage in excessive debate relying on the scriptures (pariyatti) they have heard. 'Who will speak more?' means when preaching the Dhamma, who will speak more, you or I? 'Who will speak better?' means one person may speak much but in a disconnected and unpleasant way, while another speaks in a connected and sweet way; referring to this, he said, 'Who will speak better?' One person may speak both much and well but does not speak for long and rises quickly; another can continue for a long time; referring to this point, he said, 'Who will speak longer?' The sixth sutta ends.
162:
## 7. Dutiyaovāda Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, 'faith' (saddhā) refers to the faith of conviction in the Triple Gem. 'Energy' (viriya) refers to both physical and mental energy. 'Wisdom' (paññā) refers to the wisdom that understands wholesome states. The phrase "There are no monks who give exhortation" means that for this person, there are no good friends (kalyāṇamitta) who can admonish and repeatedly instruct him; the Venerable shows that this is a cause of decline. The seventh sutta ends.

## 8. Tatiyaovāda Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, the phrase "tathā hi pana" is a particle used when presenting the reasons for former docility and current difficulty in being admonished. "Tatra" means among those elders. "What is the name of this monk?" is a question asking whether this monk is Tissa Thera or Nāga Thera. "Tatra" [in the second instance] means when such honor and offerings are being made. "Tathattāya" means for that state, specifically for the state of living in the forest and so forth. "Sabrahmacārikāma" refers to one who is called so because of desiring, longing, and praying in this way: "May these monks surround and follow me." "Tathattāya" [in the second instance] means for the purpose of generating gains and honor. "Brahmacārupaddavena" refers to being oppressed by the danger (upaddava), which is the excessive desire and lust for the four requisites of fellow practitioners. "Abhipatthanā" means excessive longing. "Brahmacāri-abhipatthanena" means by way of the four requisites, which is called the excessive longing of fellow practitioners. The eighth sutta ends.

## 9. Jhānābhiñña Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, "yāvadeva ākaṅkhāမိ" means as much as I wish. Following this, the four fine-material jhanas (rūpāvacara jhāna) are taught by way of "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" and so forth; the four immaterial attainments (arūpa samāpatti) by way of "with the complete surmounting of perceptions of forms" and so forth; the attainment of cessation (nirodha samāpatti) by way of "with the complete surmounting of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the cessation of perception and feeling"; and the five mundane direct knowledges (lokiya abhiññā) by way of "manifold forms of psychic power" and so forth. Everything that should be said regarding this text, along with the word-by-word commentary and the methods of meditation development, has already been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. In the sixth direct knowledge, "āsavānaṃ khayā" means through the destruction of the taints. "Anāsavaṃ" refers to the state of not being a condition for the taints. "Cetovimutti" refers to the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship. "Paññāvimutti" refers to the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship. The ninth sutta ends.
163:
## 10. Commentary on the Upassaya Sutta

In the tenth sutta, why does he request, "Venerable sir, please come," to go to the nunnery? He does not request it for the sake of gains and honor, but because there are nuns in this nunnery who desire meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), and he requests it to encourage them and have the meditation subjects taught. Since he himself is a learned one (tepiṭaka) who has mastered the Three Pitakas, why can he not teach it himself? It is not that he cannot. However, he requests it because he considers that the words of a Great Disciple who is like the Buddha would be more worthy of faith. In saying, "You have many duties, many things to be done," does it mean the elder was busy with construction work (navakamma) and so forth? No. After the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, the four assemblies approached the Venerable Ānanda and wept and lamented, saying, "Venerable sir, whose bowl and robes shall we take and wander now? Whose compound shall we sweep? To whom shall we offer water for washing the face?" The elder had to console the assembly, saying, "Conditioned things are impermanent; even against the body of the Blessed One, the shameless King of Death has struck. This is the nature of conditioned things; do not sorrow, do not lament." This was the elder's many duties. It was with reference to this that the Venerable Mahākassapa spoke thus. "Sandassesi" means showing the quality of practice (paṭipatti). "Samādapesi" means making them undertake (or accept). "Samuttejesi" means inspiring them. "Sampahaṃsesi" means gladdening them with the benefits attained.

"Thullatissā" means she was large in body and her name was Tissā. "Vedehamuni" means a wise sage. A wise person is called "Vedeha" because he strives in all matters with "veda," which is a term for knowledge. Being both Vedeha and a sage (muni), he is called "Vedehamuni." "Thinks he should preach the Dhamma" means that while being a forest-dweller and a rag-robe wearer herself, she intended to preach the Dhamma in the presence of the Treasurer of the Dhamma, who is a master of the Three Pitakas, thinking, "I am a Dhamma preacher." "How is this? Why is this?"—she spoke this with disregard. "Heard" means learning it according to what another person came and told. "Wait, friend Ānanda" means stay for a moment, friend. "Let not the Saṅgha examine you excessively" means let not the Bhikkhu Saṅgha investigate you for giving an excessive opportunity. This is what is meant: "Venerable Ānanda stopped a disciple who is like the Buddha but did not stop a nun; could there be an intimacy or affection with that nun?"—let not the Saṅgha think of you in this way.
164:
Now, Ven. Mahākassapa, wishing to show his equality with the Buddha, said to that bhikkhunī: "What do you think, friend?" and so on. "Sattaratana" refers to an elephant that is seven cubits in size. "Nāga" refers to an elephant. "Aḍḍhaṭṭharatana" refers to eight cubits less a half (seven and a half cubits); it means a height of seven cubits and one span, starting from the front feet up to the frontal globes (kumbha). "Tālapattikāya" means something made of young palm leaves. "Cavittha" means shifted (passed away); it does not mean dead or destroyed. Because she spoke words of blame against Ven. Mahākassapa, a great disciple who was like the Buddha, when the Elder roared a lion's roar with the six supernormal knowledges (abhiññā), her robes began to prick her whole body like thorny branches or itchy branches. At the very moment she removed those robes and put on white clothes, clarity (joy) of mind arose in that bhikkhunī. The tenth sutta is finished.

## 11. Cīvarasuttavaṇṇanā

In the eleventh sutta, "in Dakkhiṇāgiri" means: the district in the southern part of the mountain surrounding the city of Rājagaha is called Dakkhiṇāgiri; it means he was wandering in that Dakkhiṇāgiri district. Wandering (cārikā) is of two types: urgent wandering (turitacārikā) and non-urgent wandering (aturitacārikā). Among these two, urgent wandering (turitacārikā) is when a certain monk, wearing one robe and covering himself with another, carrying his bowl and robes on his shoulder and holding an umbrella, travels seven or eight yojanas in a single day with sweat pouring from his body; or when the Buddhas, seeing a being who is ready to be enlightened, travel a distance of a hundred or a thousand yojanas in a single moment. Non-urgent wandering (aturitacārikā) is the journey of one who accepts invitations for today's meal and benefits the people, traveling only a distance of a gāvuta, half a yojana, three gāvutas, or one yojana daily. This aturitacārikā is what is intended here.

Did not the Elder Ānanda follow behind the Possessor of Ten Powers like a shadow for twenty-five years, never even giving an opportunity for the words "Where is Ānanda?" to be asked? When asked at what time that Ven. Ānanda got the opportunity to wander with the Saṅgha of monks, it should be said that he got the opportunity in the year the Buddha attained Parinibbāna. It is said that after the Buddha attained Parinibbāna, Ven. Mahākassapa sat in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks who had gathered for the Buddha's Parinibbāna, selected five hundred monks for the purpose of reciting the Dhamma and Vinaya (Saṅgāyanā), and said: "Friends, we shall spend the rains retreat in Rājagaha and recite the Dhamma and Vinaya; you..."
165:
"Sever your impediments (palibodha) before the commencement of the rains retreat and gather in Rājagaha," he said, and went to Rājagaha himself. Ven. Ānanda also took the Buddha's bowl and robes, and while informing the great multitude, went to Sāvatthī; leaving from there, while going to Rājagaha, he wandered in Dakkhiṇāgiri. This was said in reference to that wandering.

"Mostly they were youths" means those who returned to the lower life (disrobed) were mostly boys, young ones, youths, monks of only one or two years, and novice boys. Why did they ordain, and why did they return to the lower life? It is said their parents thought: "Ven. Ānanda is an intimate of the Teacher; he serves him having asked for eight boons. He can take the Teacher and go to any place he wishes. Let us ordain our children in the presence of this Elder. He will bring the Teacher and come; when he comes, we will get the chance to make great offerings." For this reason, their relatives made them ordain. But when the Teacher attained Parinibbāna, that hope of theirs was cut off; then they disrobed in a single day.

"As long as they liked (yathābhirantaṃ)" means according to their own desire and inclination. "He prescribed the meal for three (tikabhojana)" is said in reference to the training rule: "In a group meal (gaṇabhojana), except on [specified] occasions, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)." In that training rule, even if three people accept and eat together an unallowable invitation, there is no offense; therefore, it is called "tikabhojana."

"To restrain the wicked" means to restrain immoral persons. "For the comfortable living of well-behaved monks" means that only by restraining the wicked can the well-behaved monks perform the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā and live in harmony; this is for the sake of their comfortable living. "Lest those of evil desires, depending on a faction, should divide the Saṅgha" means just as Devadatta, together with his following, requested and ate among families and, depending on those of evil desires, divided the Saṅgha; so too, lest other people of evil desires, forming a group and requesting and eating among families, increase their faction and, depending on that faction, divide the Saṅgha—it means he prescribed it for this reason. "And out of compassion for families" means when the Saṅgha of monks performs Uposatha and Pavāraṇā and lives in harmony, people get the opportunity to give food-by-tickets (salākabhatta) etc., and go to heaven; it means he prescribed it for the benefit of protecting the donors in this way.

"Wanders like a destroyer of crops" means wandering like one who reaps and destroys crops. "Wanders like a harasser of donors" means wandering like one who oppresses and harasses donors. "Is ruined (ullujjati)" means specifically being destroyed. "Friend Ānanda, your young monks and novices, who are mostly young and have only one or two years [of standing], are ruined," is the meaning. "Do not think of these as mere children" means this child...
166:
When the monks live in harmony, people give salāka-food and so forth, and thus they are bound for heaven. It is understood that this training rule was laid down for the sake of showing compassion to these families.

'He wanders like a destroyer of crops' means he wanders as if he were cutting and destroying crops. 'He wanders like an oppressor of families' means he wanders as if he were harming and oppressing families. 'Olujjati' means specifically to break or fall apart. 'Friend, your new monks are falling apart' means, 'Friend Ānanda, your disciples, who are mostly new monks of one or two years and young novices, are falling apart and breaking down.' 'This boy does not know his own measure'—this was said as a threat and rebuke to the Elder Mahākassapa.

'They are not free from being called boys' means they are not released from the designation of being a 'boy.' 'It is so'—this statement was made to show the reason why Venerable Ānanda deserved to be called a boy. The intention of Elder Mahākassapa here is: 'Since you wander with these young monks who are devoid of sense restraint, you, wandering with boys, deserve to be called a boy.'

'Being a former member of another sect'—this was said by the nun Thullanandā because the Elder's teacher and preceptor are not known in this Sasana, and he went forth by taking the saffron robes himself; thus, out of dissatisfaction, she wished to blame him for being a former member of another sect.

In the word 'sahasā,' the sudden arising of lust and delusion is also called 'sahasācāra' (acting impulsively). However, here it is spoken by way of the arising of anger. 'Appaṭisaṅkhā' means without reflection. Now, wishing to purify his own monkhood, Elder Mahākassapa said, 'Friend, I...' and so forth. In that text, 'to point to another teacher' means, 'I have never known pointing to anyone else as my teacher, setting aside the Blessed One.'

In the passages beginning with 'Household life is crowded,' even if a husband and wife live in a house of sixty cubits or even a hundred leagues apart, household life is still 'crowded' because of their attachment and impediments (palibodha). 'Rajāpatho' (path of dust) is said in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā to be the place where the dust of passion and so forth arises. It is also appropriate to call it the 'path of arrival' for the dust of passion. It is called 'abbhokāsa' (open air) because it is like an open space due to the absence of attachment. For a monk, even if he lives in a gabled house, a jeweled palace, or a celestial mansion with closed doors and windows, he does not cling, does not get stuck, and is not bound. Therefore...
167:
It is said, 'Going forth is like the open air.' Alternatively, household life is crowded because there is no opportunity for performing wholesome deeds. It is like a path of dust because it is a place where the dust of defilements accumulates, like a place where unswept rubbish gathers. Going forth is like the open air because there is ample opportunity to perform wholesome deeds as one pleases.

'This practice is not easy... I shall go forth'—the summary of this statement is: This noble practice of the three trainings should be practiced perfectly and completely until the final consciousness (death), without breaking it for even a single day. It should be practiced with absolute purity until the final consciousness, without being soiled by the stain of defilements for even a single day. It should be practiced as purely as a polished conch shell. To practice thus with absolute perfection is not easy for one living the household life. 'Let me shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes—the garments suitable for those practicing the noble life—and leaving the home, go forth into homelessness.' Here, the work of the household such as farming and trade is called 'agāriya.' Since such work does not exist in the state of a monk, the monkhood is to be known as 'anagāriya' (homelessness). 'Pabbajeyya' means one should practice.

'Paṭapilotikānaṃ' means of rags. Even a new cloth of thirteen cubits is called a 'rag' (pilotika) from the moment its fringes are cut off. Therefore, referring to the double-layered robe (saṃghāṭi) made by cutting up precious cloths, it is said, 'a double-layered robe made of rags.' 'Addhānamaggappaṭipanno'—a journey of half a league or more is called 'addhāna.' It means one who has entered upon such a journey, one who has entered upon a long road.

Now, to clarify how this Elder Mahākassapa went forth and how he traveled the long journey, the sequential story should be told starting from his initial aspiration. It is said that a hundred thousand aeons ago, a Teacher named Padumuttara appeared in the world. While He was residing in the Khema Deer Park near the city of Haṃsavatī, a householder named Vedeha, who possessed a wealth of eight hundred million, ate a fine meal early in the morning, undertook the Uposatha precepts, took perfumes, flowers, and so forth, went to the monastery, honored and paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down at one side. At that moment, the Teacher was addressing the third disciple, the Elder Mahānisabha, saying, 'Monks, of my...'
168:
## 
The Buddha placed the monk Nisabha in the foremost position (etadagga), declaring, "Among my disciples who are proponents of the ascetic practices (dhutavāda), this Nisabha is the foremost."

A householder, having heard this and being inspired, approached the Buddha after the Dhamma teaching when the crowd had departed. He paid homage and said, "Venerable Sir, please accept my offering of alms tomorrow." The Buddha replied, "Layman, the Saṅgha of monks is very large." "How many are there, Blessed One?" he asked. "Layman, there are six million eight hundred thousand monks," the Buddha replied. The householder then requested, "Venerable Sir, please accept the alms offering without leaving even a single novice (sāmaṇera) behind at the monastery." The Buddha accepted.

Knowing the Buddha had accepted, the householder returned home, prepared a great offering, and the next day sent word to the Buddha that it was time for the meal. The Buddha, taking His bowl and robes and surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, went to the householder’s home and sat on the prepared seat. After the pouring of the water of dedication, He accepted the gruel and other foods and performed the duties of the meal. The householder also sat near the Buddha.

In the meantime, the Elder Mahā Nisabha, while wandering for alms, arrived at that very street. Seeing the Elder, the householder rose from his seat, approached him, paid homage, and said, "Venerable Sir, please give us your bowl." The Elder gave him the bowl. The householder said, "Venerable Sir, please enter this house; the Buddha is also seated inside." The Elder replied, "Layman, it is not proper." The householder took the Elder's bowl, filled it with alms-food, brought it back out, and offered it. Then, after following the Elder for a short distance, he returned and sat near the Buddha, asking: "Venerable Sir, although I told the Elder Mahā Nisabha that the Buddha was in the house, he did not wish to enter. Does this Elder possess some special quality that is superior to Your own?"

Buddhas have no envy regarding the virtues of others. Thus, the Buddha said, "Layman, we sit in the house awaiting alms, but that monk does not sit and wait for alms in this way. We dwell in residences near villages, but he dwells only in the forest. We dwell under a roof, but he dwells only in the open air." In this manner, the Buddha described the Elder's various virtues as if filling the great ocean. The householder, who was already like a burning lamp, became even more inspired, as if oil had been poured on it. He thought, "What use is other wealth and prosperity to me? In the future, I shall make a wish to become the foremost among those who practice the dhutanga under a Buddha."

That householder invited the Buddha again and gave offerings in that same manner for seven days. On the seventh day, he offered sets of triple robes (ticīvara) to the six million eight hundred thousand monks, prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, and said: "Venerable Sir, as I have been giving alms for these seven days..."
169:
## 
"...I have performed bodily, verbal, and mental actions accompanied by loving-kindness (metta). By this merit, I do not wish for any other heavenly prosperity, nor the status of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā. Rather, may this deed of mine be a condition for attaining the same position achieved by the Elder Mahā Nisabha and for becoming the foremost among the practitioners of the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutanga) in the presence of a future Buddha."

The Buddha, reflecting, "This man has wished for a great position; will it be fulfilled?" saw that it would be fulfilled and said, "The position you have wished for is delightful. In the future, one hundred thousand aeons (kappas) from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. You will be His third disciple, known as the Elder Mahā Kassapa."

Hearing this prophecy, the householder believed that "Buddhas do not speak two words" (their word is never false) and regarded that attainment as if he would receive it the very next day. He guarded his virtue (sīla) for the rest of his life and, after passing away, was reborn in heaven.

From then on, while experiencing prosperity in the worlds of gods and humans, ninety-one aeons ago from this present Bhadda Kappa, when the Buddha Vipassī was staying at the Khema Deer Park near the city of Bandhumatī, he passed away from the deva world and was reborn into a certain poor Brahmin family. At that time, a great stir arose: "The Blessed One Vipassī will preach the Dhamma once every seven years." Deities throughout the whole of Jambudīpa announced, "The Teacher will preach the Dhamma," and the Brahmin heard this news.

That Brahmin had only one lower garment, and the Brahmin woman (his wife) was the same. For an upper robe, however, they had only one between the two of them. Thus, he was known throughout the city as "Ekasāṭaka" (the One-Robe Brahmin). When there was a gathering for Brahmins, he would leave his wife at home and go himself. When there was a gathering for Brahmin women, he would stay at home and his wife would go, wearing that robe. On that day, the Brahmin asked his wife, "My dear, will you listen to the Dhamma at night or during the day?" She replied, "We womenfolk cannot go to listen at night; I will listen during the day." So, leaving her husband at home and wearing the robe, she went with other laywomen during the day, paid homage to the Teacher, sat in a suitable place, listened to the Dhamma, and returned with the laywomen. Then the Brahmin, leaving his wife at home and wearing the robe, went to the monastery.

At that time, the Teacher was seated upon the decorated Dhamma-seat in the midst of the assembly. Holding a fan, He preached the Dhamma as if bringing down the celestial Ganges or as if churning the great ocean using Mount Sineru as a churning stick. As the Brahmin sat at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, the five types of joy (pīti) arose, pervading his entire body during the first watch of the night. He thought of folding his robe and offering it to the Buddha. After thinking this, many disadvantages of not giving occurred to him, and a stingy, selfish mind (macchariya) arose again. "My wife and I have only this one upper robe. There is no other to wear. To go outside without an upper robe is..."
170:
The Buddha preached the Dhamma as if he were churning the Great Ocean using Mount Sineru as a churning stick. To that Brahmin sitting at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, in the very first watch of the night, fivefold joy arose, pervading his entire body. The Brahmin folded the cloak he was wearing and thought, "I will offer this to the Buddha." Then, stinginess arose in him, showing thousands of disadvantages. He thought, "There is only one cloak for my wife and me; there is no other wrap. It is impossible to go outside without an upper wrap." Thus, he became unwilling to give in every way.

Then, when the first watch had passed and in the middle watch also, joy arose in the same way. He thought the same and remained unwilling to give. Then, when the middle watch had passed and in the last watch also, joy arose in the same way. The Brahmin resolved, "Let there be defeat or let there be death, I will deal with it later," folded the cloth, and placed it at the Teacher's feet. Then, bending his left arm and striking it with his right hand three times, he shouted three times, "I have won! I have won!"

At that time, King Bandhuma was listening to the Dhamma, sitting behind a curtain behind the Dhamma-seat. It is the nature of kings not to like the sound "I have won." The King sent a man, saying, "Go, ask that man what he is saying." The man went and asked, and the Brahmin replied, "Others conquer enemy armies by mounting elephants, horses, and so on, and by taking swords, weapons, and so on. That victory is not wonderful. But I, as if breaking the head of a fierce, rogue bull coming from behind with a club and making it flee, have crushed the mind of stinginess and offered my wrap to the Ten-Powered One. I have conquered that stinginess."

The man went and reported this matter to the King. The King said, "Friends, we did not know what was worthy of the Ten-Powered One, but the Brahmin knew," and sent a pair of garments as a gift. Seeing the garments, the Brahmin thought, "This King gave nothing to me while I sat silently, but gave only when I spoke of the Teacher's virtues. What use is this to me, which was obtained because of the Teacher's virtues?" and offered that pair of garments also to the Buddha. The King asked, "What did the Brahmin do?" and hearing that he gave that pair also to the Tathāgata, he sent two more pairs. He offered those too. The King sent four pairs, and so on, up to thirty-two pairs of garments. Then—
171:
The Brahmin, thinking, "Taking this by increasing it further would be in vain," took two pairs of garments—one for himself and one for his wife—and offered the remaining thirty pairs to the Tathāgata. From then on, he became an intimate devotee of the Teacher.

Furthermore, one day during the cold season, King Bandhuma saw the Brahmin listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher and gave him his own red woolen blanket worth a hundred thousand, saying, "From today onwards, wear this blanket and listen to the Dhamma." The Brahmin thought, "What is the use of wearing this blanket on this foul body?" and having made it into a canopy over the Tathāgata’s bed inside the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), he departed. Then one day, the King went to the monastery early in the morning and sat in the presence of the Teacher inside the Gandhakuṭi. At that time, the six-colored rays of the Buddha struck the red blanket canopy, making it shine exceedingly. The King, looking up, recognized it and said, "Venerable Sir, this is our blanket, given by us to the Brahmin Ekasāṭaka."

The Buddha said, "Great King, you honored the Brahmin, and the Brahmin honored me." The King, thinking, "The Brahmin knew what was appropriate, but we did not," was greatly inspired. He gave the gift known as the Sabbaṭṭhaka (The Gift of All Eights), providing eight of every kind of useful item for humans, and appointed the Brahmin to the position of Royal Chaplain (Purohita). The Brahmin, thinking, "Eight times eight is sixty-four," established sixty-four ticket-meals (salākabhatta) and gave alms for the rest of his life. Having guarded his virtue, he passed away and was reborn in heaven.

Passing away from there, he was reborn in this eon in a wealthy family in Bārāṇasī, during the interval between the Buddhas Koṇāgamana and Kassapa. When he reached adulthood and was living as a householder, one day he was walking on foot in the forest. At that time, a Paccekabuddha was sewing a robe on a riverbank and was about to fold it up because the material for the border (anuvāta) was insufficient. Seeing this, the householder asked, "Venerable Sir, why are you folding it up?" When told it was because the border material was insufficient, he offered a cloth, saying, "Venerable Sir, please use this," and made a wish: "In every place I am reborn, may I never suffer deficiency in anything." Meanwhile, at his home, while his sister and wife were quarreling, the Paccekabuddha entered for alms.
172:
At that time, the householder's sister, having offered alms-food to the Paccekabuddha, made a wish concerning the householder's wife: "May I be spared from such a fool even from a hundred leagues away." The wife, standing at the door, heard this and thought, "May this monk not eat the food given by this woman." She took the bowl, threw away the alms-food, filled it with mud, and offered it. Seeing this, the sister said, "You foolish woman, abuse me or strike me instead. It is not proper to throw away the food from the bowl of a Paccekabuddha, who has fulfilled the perfections for two incalculable eons, and give him mud."

Then, remorse (reflection) arose in the wife. She said, "Please wait a moment, Bhante," threw away the mud, washed the bowl, rubbed it with scented powder, filled it with excellent catumadhura (four sweets), poured ghee the color of a lotus heart on top, and placed the radiant bowl in the Paccekabuddha's hand. She made a wish: "Just as this alms-food is radiant, may my body also be radiant." The Paccekabuddha gave a blessing and flew into the sky. The husband and wife performed meritorious deeds throughout their lives and were reborn in heaven. When they passed away from there, the lay devotee was reborn in Bārāṇasī as the son of a merchant with a wealth of eighty crores, and the other was reborn as the daughter of a similar merchant.

When the merchant's son reached maturity, they brought that same merchant's daughter to him. Due to the power of that past deed which had not yet yielded its result, as soon as she entered her husband's house and reached the threshold, her whole body emitted a foul odor like an open latrine (vacca-kuṭi). The merchant's son asked, "Whose smell is this?" and hearing it was the merchant's daughter's, he said, "Take her away, take her away!" and sent her back to her parents' house just as she had been brought. In this manner, she was rejected and sent back from seven places. She thought, "I have been rejected from seven places. What is the use of my life?"

She had her jewelry broken down and made into a golden brick, one cubit (ratana) long, one span wide, and four finger-breadths thick. Then, taking a mass of orpiment (haritāla) and realgar (manosilā) and eight handfuls of lotuses, she went to the site where the stupa of Kassapa the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) was being built. At that moment, as a row of bricks was being laid, one brick was missing at the junction. The merchant's daughter said to the mason, "Please place this brick here." The mason said, "Dear daughter, you have come at a good time; place it yourself." She climbed up, mixed the orpiment and realgar with oil, and firmly set the golden brick with that mortar...
173:
Having made an offering with eight handfuls of lotuses on top (of the brick) and paid homage, she made a wish: "Wherever I am reborn, may the scent of sandalwood waft from my body and the scent of blue lotuses from my mouth." After paying homage to the stupa and circumambulating it clockwise (padakkhiṇa), she departed.

At that very moment, the merchant's son who had first brought her to his house remembered her. A festival was also being proclaimed in the city. He asked his attendants, "There was a merchant's daughter who was brought here then; where is she?" "Lord, she is at her parents' house," they replied. "Bring her here; we shall celebrate the festival together," he said. They went and stood there, paying homage to her. When she asked, "Friends, why have you come?" they told her the reason. "Friends, I have offered my jewelry to the stupa; I have no ornaments to wear," she said. They went back and informed the merchant's son. "Bring her; she will obtain ornaments," he said. They brought her. As soon as she entered the house, the scent of sandalwood and the scent of blue lotuses wafted through the entire house.

The merchant's son asked her, "Previously, a foul odor wafted from your body, but now the scent of sandalwood wafts from your body and the scent of blue lotuses from your mouth. How is this?" She told him of her deeds from the beginning. The merchant's son, being inspired, thinking, "The teaching of the Buddhas is indeed a means of deliverance from suffering," covered the one-league-high golden stupa with a woolen mantle and decorated it here and there with golden lotuses the size of chariot wheels. Those golden lotuses had tassels twelve cubits long. He remained in that life until the end of his days and was reborn in heaven. Passing away from there, he was reborn in a certain minister's family in a place about one league from Bārāṇasī. The merchant's daughter also passed away from the deva world and was reborn as the eldest daughter in a royal family.

When they reached maturity, a festival was proclaimed in the village where the young man lived. The young man said to his mother, "Mother, give me a lower garment (paso); I will play at the festival." The mother took out a washed cloth and gave it to him. "Mother, this cloth is too coarse," he said. She took out another and gave it; he rejected that too. She took out another and gave it; he rejected that as well. Then the mother said to her son, "Dear son, in the kind of house we were born into, we do not have the merit to obtain a cloth finer than this." "Mother, I will go to a place where it can be obtained," he said. "My son, even this very day I wish for you to obtain the kingship in the city of Bārāṇasī," she said. He paid homage to his mother and said, "Mother, I am going." "Go, dear son," she said. It is said that his mother's mind was...
174:
The thought occurred to him (regarding his mother): "Where will she go? She will stay in this house or in this place." Driven by the power of his merit, he departed and reached the city of Bārāṇasī, where he lay down on the auspicious stone slab in the royal garden, covering himself entirely, including his head. That day was the seventh day after the King of Bārāṇasī had passed away.

After performing the funeral rites for the king, the ministers gathered in the royal courtyard and consulted together: "The king had only one daughter and no son. A kingdom without a king cannot endure. Who is worthy to be king?" They urged one another, saying, "You be the king! You be the king!" The court chaplain (purohita) said, "It is not proper to search extensively. Let us release the festive chariot (phussaratha)." The ministers harnessed four Sindh horses the color of white water-lilies, placed the five royal regalia and the white parasol upon the chariot, released it, and had musical instruments played behind it. The chariot departed through the eastern gate and headed toward the royal garden. Some said, "It is going toward the garden out of habit; let us turn back." But the chaplain said, "Do not turn back." The chariot circled the young man clockwise and came to a halt, ready for him to mount. The chaplain pulled back the edge of the covering and examined the soles of his feet. He said, "Let alone this Jambudīpa; this man is worthy to rule even over the four great islands with their two thousand surrounding small islands." He then ordered the musical instruments to be played again and again, three times in total.

Then the young man uncovered his face, looked out, and asked, "For what purpose have you come?" They replied, "Sire, the kingship has come to you." He asked, "Where is the king?" They answered, "Sire, our lord has passed away." "How many days have passed?" "Today is the seventh day." "Is there no son or daughter?" "There is a daughter, Sire, but no son." "In that case, I shall rule," he accepted. Right then, the ministers built a consecration pavilion, adorned the princess with all her ornaments, brought her to the garden, and performed the consecration of the young man.

After the consecration, they presented him with a garment worth a hundred thousand. The king asked, "Ministers, what is this?" They replied, "Sire, it is a royal robe." "Ministers, is it not coarse?" he remarked. They replied, "Sire, among the garments used by humans, there is none finer or better than this." He asked, "Did your king wear such a garment?" "Yes, Sire," they replied. "I do not think your king was a man of great merit..."
175:
He said, "Bring the golden water-pitcher; we shall obtain royal robes." The attendants brought the golden pitcher. The king rose, washed his hands, rinsed his mouth, took water in his hand, and sprinkled it toward the east. Splitting the solid earth, eight wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavrikshas) sprang up. Again taking water, he sprinkled it in the four directions—south, west, and north—in the same manner. In each direction, eight trees appeared, totaling thirty-two wish-fulfilling trees. The king donned one celestial robe and wrapped another around himself. He then gave the order: "Let it be proclaimed by drum throughout King Nanda's realm that women who spin should spin no more thread." He then had the white parasol raised, mounted the back of a noble, decorated elephant, entered the city, ascended the palace, and enjoyed great royal splendor.

As time passed, one day the queen, seeing the king's splendor, showed a compassionate expression, saying, "Oh, what a pity!" When asked, "Queen, why is this?" she replied, "Sire, your splendor is very great. In the past, you had faith in the Buddhas and performed good deeds. But now, you are not performing the meritorious deeds that are the cause for the future life." "To whom shall I give? There are no virtuous ones," he said. "Sire, Jambudīpa is not empty of Arahants. You just prepare the offerings; I will find the Arahants," she replied. The next day, the king prepared offerings at the eastern gate. Early in the morning, the queen undertook the Uposatha precepts, and lying prostrate on her breast facing east on the upper palace, she said, "If there are Arahants in this direction, may they come and accept our alms." There were no Arahants in that direction. They gave those offerings to the poor, travelers, and beggars.

The next day, they prepared offerings at the southern gate and did the same; the following day at the western gate. On the day they prepared offerings at the northern gate, while the queen was inviting them in the same manner, the Great Paduma Paccekabuddha, the eldest of the five hundred Paccekabuddhas who were the sons of Padumavatī living in the Himālaya, addressed his brothers: "Sirs, King Nanda is inviting you. Accept his offering." Having accepted, the next day they washed their faces at Lake Anotatta, traveled through the air, and descended at the northern gate. People went and informed the king, "Sire, five hundred Paccekabuddhas have arrived." The king, together with the queen, went and paid homage, took their bowls, invited the Paccekabuddhas up to the palace, and gave them offerings. When the meal was finished...
176: The King prostrated at the feet of the Elder of the Sangha, and the Queen at the feet of the junior monk of the Sangha, saying, "May the Venerable Ones not suffer for lack of the four requisites; may we not decline in merit. Please give us your word to reside here for the rest of your lives." Having secured their promise, they prepared five hundred leaf-roofed huts and five hundred walkways in the royal garden, complete in every detail, and had them reside there. As time passed, a rebellion broke out at the border of the King's country. The King, after advising the Queen, "I am going to pacify the border; do not be negligent toward the Paccekabuddhas," departed. Before the King's return, the life-force of the Paccekabuddhas was exhausted. The Paccekabuddha Mahāpaduma, having spent the three watches of the night in the sport of meditative absorption (jhāna), at dawn, while standing and leaning against a support board, attained Parinibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without remainder. In this manner, all the remaining Venerable Ones also attained Parinibbāna. On the following day, the Queen had the sitting area of the Paccekabuddhas smeared with cow dung, scattered flowers, and offered incense. While waiting for the arrival of the Venerable Ones and not seeing them come, she sent a servant, saying, "Go, dear man, find out if anything is unwell with the Venerable Ones." He went and opened the door of Mahāpaduma's leaf hut. Not seeing him there, he went to the walkway and saw him standing leaning against the support board. He paid homage and said, "Venerable Sir, it is time [to come]." How could a body that has attained Parinibbāna speak? Thinking, "He must be asleep," he approached and touched the tops of the feet with his hand. Realizing from the coldness and stiffness of the feet that he had attained Parinibbāna, he went to the second and then the third, and so on. Knowing that all had attained Parinibbāna, he returned to the palace. When asked, "Dear man, where are the Paccekabuddhas?" he replied, "Your Majesty, they have attained Parinibbāna." The Queen, weeping and lamenting, went there with the city folk, performed the funeral honors, carried out the final rites for the Paccekabuddhas, took the relics, and enshrined them in a stupa. When the King returned after pacifying the border, he asked the Queen who came to meet him, "Dear lady, were you not negligent toward the Paccekabuddhas? Are the Venerable Ones free from illness?" She replied, "Great King, the Lords have attained Parinibbāna." The King thought, "Even for such wise ones as these, death arises; how can there be escape for us?" Without entering the city, he entered the garden, summoned his eldest son, handed over the kingdom to him, and himself ordained as a monk.
177: The Queen also thought, "Now that this King has ordained, what shall I do?" and ordained in that very garden. Both of them, having developed meditative absorption (jhāna), when they passed away from that life, were reborn in the Brahma realm. While they were residing in that Brahma realm, our Teacher appeared in the world, set the noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, and in due course entered Rājagaha. This youth Pippali was born in the womb of the chief consort of the Brahmin Kapila in the Brahmin village of Mahātittha in the country of Magadha. This Bhaddā Kāpilānī was born in the womb of the chief consort of a Brahmin of the Kosiya clan in the city of Sāgala in the country of Madda. As they grew up in due course, when the youth Pippali reached the age of twenty and Bhaddā reached the age of sixteen, the parents looked at their son and urged him strongly, saying, "Dear son, you have reached the proper age; you should establish the family line." The youth said, "Do not speak such words in my hearing. As long as you are alive, I will look after you. Only after you have passed away will I go forth and ordain." After a few days had passed, the parents urged him again, and he refused in the same way. They urged him again, and he refused again. From then on, the mother spoke and urged him continuously. The youth thought, "I will make my mother understand," and giving a thousand nikkhas of red gold, he had goldsmiths make a statue of a woman. When the polishing and other work on the statue were finished, he had it dressed in red cloth, adorned with beautiful flowers and various ornaments, and then summoned his mother, saying, "Mother, if I find a woman with such an appearance, I will stay in the house; if I do not find one, I will not stay." The wise Brahmin woman thought, "My son is one of great merit, who has given gifts and made resolutions. When performing merit, he did not do it alone. Surely there must be a woman with an appearance like this golden statue who performed merit together with him." She summoned eight Brahmins, satisfied them with all they desired, placed the golden statue on a carriage, and sent them off, saying, "Go, dear sirs. If you find a maiden of this kind in a family equal to ours in birth, clan, and wealth, give this golden statue itself as a gift." Those Brahmins said, "This is indeed our task," and departed. Thinking, "Where shall we go?" they decided, "The country of Madda is a source of beautiful women; let us go to the country of Madda," and went to the city of Sāgala in the country of Madda. In that city, they placed the golden statue at the river landing and stayed in a certain place. At that time, Bhaddā's nurse, having bathed Bhaddā, adorned her, and seated her in the auspicious chamber, came to bathe herself. Seeing the statue, she mistook it, thinking, "My mistress has come here!" and scolded it, saying, "Hey, you wicked girl, have you come here like this?" and struck the cheek of the golden statue with the edge of her palm. Her hand immediately throbbed as if it had struck a stone. Then the nurse stepped back and realized, "This statue of such great majesty is [like] my mistress." Indeed, she said this statue was not even fit to receive the change of clothes of her mistress. Then those men surrounded the nurse and asked, "Does your mistress have an appearance like this?" The nurse replied, "What are you saying? More than a hundred times [more beautiful] than this statue..."
178:
They went to the city of Sāgala. There, they placed the golden statue at a bathing ghat and sat down to one side. Then, Bhaddā's nurse, having bathed and adorned Bhaddā and seated her in the auspicious chamber, came to bathe herself. Seeing the statue and thinking, "My mistress has come here," she threatened it out of recognition and scolded it, saying, "You wicked woman, why have you come here?" Raising the edge of her palm, she said, "Go away quickly!" and struck its cheek. Her hand shook as if it had struck a stone. She stepped back and said, "Seeing such a firm and majestic form, I mistakenly thought, 'It is my mistress.' Indeed, this statue is not even worthy to receive my mistress's garments." Then the people surrounded her and asked, "Is your mistress of such an appearance?" She replied, "What is this statue? Our mistress is a hundred times, even a thousand times more beautiful than this. When she sits in a chamber twelve cubits wide, there is no need to light a lamp; she dispels the darkness by the radiance of her body alone." Saying, "If that is so, come along," they took the hunchbacked nurse, placed the golden statue on a carriage, and stood at the door of the house of the treasurer of the Kosiya clan, announcing their arrival.

The Kosiya Brahmin welcomed them and asked, "Where have you come from?" They replied, "From the house of the Brahmin Kapila in the village of Mahātittha in the kingdom of Magadha." He asked, "For what reason have you come?" They explained the reason. He said, "Friends, it is well. The Brahmin is of equal birth, clan, and wealth to us; I shall give the maiden." He then accepted the gifts.

They sent word to the Brahmin Kapila, saying, "The maiden has been found; perform what needs to be done." Hearing this news, they told the young Pipphali, "The maiden has been found." The young man thought, "I thought I would not get one, but these people say they have found one. I will send a letter saying I have no desire for this." He went to a secluded place and wrote a letter: "Let Bhaddā find a household life suitable to her birth, clan, and wealth. As for me, I shall leave and ordain. Let her not be remorseful later." Bhaddā also, hearing "They wish to give me to such-and-such a person," went to a secluded place and wrote a letter: "Let the noble son find a household life suitable to his birth, clan, and wealth. As for me, I shall ordain. Let him not be remorseful later."

Both letters met on the way. When asked, "Whose letter is this?" they said, "It is a letter sent by the young Pipphali to Bhaddā." When asked, "To whom is this letter sent?" they said, "It is a letter sent by Bhaddā to the young Pipphali." Having said this, they read both letters, and saying, "Look at the behavior of these children," they tore them up and in the forest...
179:
...discarding [the original letters], they wrote identical letters and sent them to both sides. In this way, the union of those two occurred, even though they were unwilling.

On that very wedding day, the young Pipphali had a flower garland made, and Bhaddā also had one made. Having placed those garlands in the middle of the seat, after eating their evening meal, they both came together, thinking, "We shall ascend the couch." The young man ascended the couch from the right side. Bhaddā ascended from the left side and said, "On whichever side the flowers wither, let it be known that a thought of lust has arisen in that person. This flower garland must not be touched." Fearing physical contact with each other, they passed the three watches of the night without falling asleep. During the day, there was not even a mere smile. Without being entangled in sensual pleasures, they did not manage the household affairs as long as their parents were alive; they only took charge after their parents had passed away.

The wealth of the young Pipphali was immense. The gold dust alone, which was discarded after being rubbed on his body each day, amounted to about twelve measures (nāḷi) by the Magadhan standard. There were sixty large reservoirs constructed with machinery, a workplace spanning twelve leagues (yojana), fourteen villages of servants the size of Anurādhapura, fourteen elephant units, fourteen cavalry units, and fourteen chariot units.

One day, the young Pipphali, mounted on an adorned horse and surrounded by a great crowd, went to the workplace.
